stem: A 60-year-old female presents with inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. Where is the site of the lesion?
explanation: Visual field defects: Superior homonymous quadrantanopia = temporal lobe (Meyer's loop — 'pie in the sky'). Inferior homonymous quadrantanopia = parietal lobe (superior optic radiation). Complete homonymous hemianopia = occipital lobe. Remember: Parietal = inferior; Temporal = superior.

stem: Fabry disease is an X-linked recessive disorder. In which organelle is the defective enzyme located?
explanation: Fabry disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A (GLA gene, X-linked), leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in lysosomes of vascular endothelium and other cells. Features: angiokeratomas, neuropathic pain (acroparaesthesiae), corneal opacities, renal failure, cardiomyopathy, stroke. Treatment: enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase).

stem: What is the breakthrough dose calculation for opioids in palliative care?
explanation: Breakthrough (PRN) dose = 1/6th of the total daily opioid dose. This can be given every 4 hours as needed. E.g., if total daily oral morphine is 60mg/day, breakthrough dose = 10mg oral morphine. If on SC infusion of 30mg/24hr, breakthrough SC dose = 5mg. Review after 24 hours and adjust regular dose if ≥3 breakthrough doses used.

stem: A patient presents with features of acromegaly. What is the confirmatory diagnostic test?
explanation: Acromegaly (excess GH, usually from pituitary adenoma) is confirmed by OGTT: after oral glucose load (75g), GH should suppress to <1 mU/L in normal individuals. In acromegaly, GH fails to suppress (paradoxical rise may occur). IGF-1 is used as a screening test (elevated in acromegaly). MRI pituitary is done to localise the adenoma after biochemical confirmation.

stem: What is the mode of action of the combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP)?
explanation: The combined OCP (oestrogen + progestogen) primarily works by inhibiting the LH surge (via negative feedback on hypothalamus/pituitary), thereby preventing ovulation. Secondary mechanisms: thickening of cervical mucus (preventing sperm penetration) and thinning of endometrium (preventing implantation). The primary mechanism for efficacy is ovulation inhibition.

stem: A patient presents with haemoptysis, raised creatinine and sinusitis. Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
explanation: The triad of upper respiratory tract (sinusitis, saddle-nose deformity), lower respiratory tract (haemoptysis, pulmonary infiltrates), and renal involvement (RPGN, raised creatinine) is classic for GPA (Wegener's granulomatosis). c-ANCA (anti-PR3) is positive in ~90% of generalised GPA. p-ANCA (anti-MPO) is associated with MPA and eosinophilic GPA (Churg-Strauss).

stem: A patient presents with pain and tenderness at the base of the thumb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: De Quervain's tenosynovitis affects the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons in the first dorsal compartment of the wrist. It presents with pain and tenderness over the radial styloid and first extensor compartment. Finkelstein's test is positive (pain on ulnar deviation of wrist with thumb tucked in fist). Common in new mothers and those performing repetitive thumb movements.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Oseltamivir?
explanation: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and Zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors. Neuraminidase is an influenza surface enzyme that cleaves sialic acid residues, allowing newly formed virus particles to be released from infected cells. Inhibition prevents viral spread. Most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Active against influenza A and B. M2 blockers (amantadine) only work against influenza A.

stem: A family has a history of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Two brothers have the positive gene, but the mother tests negative. What is the mode of inheritance?
explanation: DMD is X-linked recessive. If two brothers are affected but the mother tests negative (no mutation in blood), the explanation is gonadal (germline) mosaicism — the mutation occurred in a proportion of the mother's germ cells but not her somatic cells. This means genetic testing of blood is negative but she can still pass the mutation to offspring. Gonadal mosaicism accounts for ~10-15% of de novo DMD cases.

stem: A patient on TPN who has been NPO for several days develops heart failure and muscle weakness. What is the most likely electrolyte abnormality?
explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition (especially carbohydrates) is reintroduced after prolonged starvation. Glucose causes insulin release → cellular uptake of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium → severe hypophosphataemia. Hypophosphataemia causes: heart failure, respiratory failure, muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, haemolytic anaemia, and encephalopathy. Prevention: check and correct electrolytes before refeeding; start slowly.

stem: A patient with a history of asthma presents with difficulty eating and drinking. Endoscopic biopsy shows eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: EoE is an allergic/immune-mediated condition characterised by eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal mucosa (>15 eosinophils/HPF on biopsy). Strongly associated with atopic conditions (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis). Presents with dysphagia, food impaction, heartburn. Endoscopy: trachealization/rings, linear furrows, whitish exudates. Treatment: dietary elimination, PPI, topical steroids (swallowed fluticasone/budesonide).

stem: A patient has 12 months of diarrhoea worsening with NSAIDs, small joint and knee pain/arthritis, and reduced forward flexion. RA factor is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Crohn's disease (CD) can affect any part of the GI tract and is associated with extraintestinal manifestations including seronegative arthritis (peripheral and axial/spondylitic). NSAIDs worsen IBD (increase flares). Seronegative arthropathy + chronic diarrhoea worsened by NSAIDs + axial symptoms (reduced flexion) points to CD-associated spondyloarthropathy. Unlike AS, CD-associated sacroiliitis is often asymmetric.

stem: An elderly male presents with bone pain and raised ALP. What is the next investigation?
explanation: Paget's disease of bone presents in elderly patients with bone pain, deformity, and markedly raised ALP (often >1000 IU/L) with normal calcium and phosphate. Bone scan (isotope bone scintigraphy) is the most sensitive investigation to assess extent of disease and identify active lesions ('hot spots'). X-rays show characteristic changes (blade of grass, cotton-wool skull). Treatment: bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid).

stem: A 30-year-old female trying to conceive has routine ACR 200 mg/g and hypertension. Which antihypertensive should be chosen?
explanation: In a woman trying to conceive or in pregnancy, ACEi/ARBs (losartan) are CONTRAINDICATED (teratogenic — renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios). Labetalol (alpha + beta blocker) is the preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy and for women planning conception. Methyldopa and nifedipine are also safe in pregnancy. Indapamide and amlodipine are not preferred in pregnancy.

stem: A pregnant lady with Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome (APAS). What is the treatment?
explanation: In APAS during pregnancy: LMWH + low-dose aspirin is standard treatment to prevent thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss (miscarriage, stillbirth, pre-eclampsia). Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester. LMWH does not cross the placenta. Treatment is usually continued throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum.

stem: DIC scenario — which chromosomal translocation is associated with APML (Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia)?
explanation: APML (AML M3) is characterised by t(15;17) translocation, creating the PML-RARA fusion gene. RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha) fusion blocks differentiation of promyelocytes. APML classically presents with DIC due to release of procoagulant granules from leukaemic cells. Treatment: ATRA (All-Trans Retinoic Acid) + arsenic trioxide — induces differentiation of blasts.

stem: What is the anticoagulation choice in a patient with AF and mechanical mitral valve replacement?
explanation: Mechanical heart valves (especially mitral position) require lifelong warfarin anticoagulation. DOACs (NOACs) are CONTRAINDICATED in mechanical valve replacement — the RE-ALIGN trial showed dabigatran was associated with higher rates of thromboembolic events and bleeding compared to warfarin in mechanical valve patients. Target INR for mitral mechanical valve: 2.5-3.5.

stem: A patient presents with pansystolic murmur at the apex and AF. Echo shows left atrial dilatation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: MR presents with: pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, AF (due to left atrial dilatation from volume overload), and left atrial dilatation on echo. Left ventricular dilatation also occurs due to volume overload. Causes: MVP, rheumatic heart disease, ischaemic MR, dilated cardiomyopathy. Mitral stenosis causes mid-diastolic murmur with loud S1.

stem: A patient has high BP, low Na+ and low K+. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism — usually aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma) presents with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and hypernatraemia (or normal Na+). Excess aldosterone causes Na+ and water retention (HTN) and K+ excretion (hypokalaemia). Metabolic alkalosis also occurs. Investigations: aldosterone:renin ratio (elevated), CT/MRI adrenals, adrenal vein sampling. Treatment: adrenalectomy (adenoma) or spironolactone (bilateral hyperplasia).

stem: A patient presents with itching, red rash and multiple vesicles/blisters. What is the treatment?
explanation: The presentation of itchy red rash with vesicles/blisters is characteristic of Varicella (chickenpox) or Herpes Zoster (shingles). Treatment: Aciclovir (antivirals). For chickenpox: oral aciclovir if >14 years (higher risk of complications). For shingles: oral aciclovir/valaciclovir/famciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset. Reduces severity and duration, and risk of postherpetic neuralgia.

stem: A patient presents with lateral medullary syndrome. Which artery is occluded?
explanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by occlusion of the vertebral artery or PICA. Features (PICA mnemonic): Ipsilateral: facial pain/numbness (V), Horner's syndrome, cerebellar signs, dysphagia/dysarthria (IX,X). Contralateral: spinothalamic loss (pain/temperature) in limbs/trunk. Classic: crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body).

stem: What is the formula for NNT (Number Needed to Treat)?
explanation: NNT = 1 / Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR). ARR = Control Event Rate (CER) - Experimental Event Rate (EER). A lower NNT means a more effective treatment. NNT of 1 = every patient treated benefits. For harm, the equivalent is NNH (Number Needed to Harm) = 1/ARI (Absolute Risk Increase).

stem: What is the formula for Positive Predictive Value (PPV)?
explanation: PPV is the probability that a person with a positive test truly has the disease. It depends heavily on prevalence (pre-test probability). In high-prevalence populations, PPV is higher for the same test. Simple form: PPV = TP / (TP + FP). NPV = TN / (TN + FN). Both are prevalence-dependent, unlike sensitivity and specificity.

stem: What is the conversion ratio from oral morphine to subcutaneous morphine?
explanation: Oral morphine to subcutaneous (SC) morphine: divide the total daily oral morphine dose by 2 to get the equivalent SC dose (because SC bioavailability is approximately twice that of oral morphine due to first-pass metabolism). E.g., Oral morphine 60mg/24hr → SC morphine 30mg/24hr via syringe driver.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with confusion, constipation, thirst. Labs show high urea & creatinine, normal Na+ and K+. CT brain shows no metastasis. Neurological exam is normal. What is the next best investigation?
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma can cause hypercalcaemia (paraneoplastic syndrome), which explains confusion, constipation, thirst (symptoms of hypercalcaemia - 'bones, stones, groans, moans'). Serum calcium is the next best investigation.

stem: What is the classic auscultatory finding in Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)?
explanation: In ASD, the right heart is volume overloaded, causing delayed pulmonary valve closure. This splitting does not vary with respiration (fixed), unlike normal physiological splitting. Fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of ASD.

stem: A patient presents with low cortisol, episodes of hypoglycaemia consistent with Addison's disease. What is the diagnostic test?
explanation: The Short Synacthen Test (SST) is the gold standard for diagnosing primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). It measures cortisol response 30-60 minutes after synthetic ACTH (Synacthen) administration. A blunted response confirms the diagnosis.

stem: A 26-year-old female with intermenstrual bleeding on OCP. Investigation reveals Chlamydia positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: First-line treatment for uncomplicated Chlamydia trachomatis infection is Azithromycin 1g single dose OR Doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days. Azithromycin is preferred for compliance. Intermenstrual bleeding on OCP is a classic presentation of chlamydial cervicitis.

stem: A 45-year-old female on ACEi for 4 weeks has raised potassium (hyperkalaemia). She has a history of DM and CKD. What is the most likely cause of her hyperkalaemia?
options: Decreased K+ secretion in loop of Henle
Decreased aldosterone effect on collecting duct
Decreased GFR causing reduced K+ filtration
explanation: ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to II, reducing aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone normally promotes Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in the collecting duct. With reduced aldosterone, K+ secretion decreases, causing hyperkalaemia. This is compounded by CKD and DM (type 4 RTA).

stem: A 41-year-old man presents with rapidly progressing dementia and movement disorder. EEG shows periodic triphasic sharp waves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sporadic CJD presents with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, and visual disturbances. The hallmark EEG finding is periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) / triphasic sharp waves. CSF 14-3-3 protein is also a useful marker. sCJD is the most common form (~85% of CJD cases).

stem: A patient presents with pain on heels and soles while walking, anterior knee and thigh pain with weakness. What is the underlying neurological level?
explanation: S1 nerve root supplies: sensation to the lateral foot and sole, plantar flexion (gastrocnemius/soleus), and the ankle jerk reflex. Pain along the sole and heel with weakness is characteristic of S1 radiculopathy. L3/L4 would cause anterior thigh/knee symptoms predominantly.

stem: Which ECG finding is associated with hypokalaemia?
explanation: Hypokalaemia classically causes U waves on ECG (a positive deflection after the T wave, best seen in V2-V3), flattening or inversion of T waves, and ST depression. Severe hypokalaemia can cause arrhythmias. U waves represent delayed repolarisation of Purkinje fibres.

stem: A young person presents with severe backache. Forward flexion is limited due to pain. Symptoms improve with ibuprofen, rest and physiotherapy. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Herniated disc (prolapsed intervertebral disc) typically presents in young adults with acute back pain, limited flexion, and radiculopathy. It responds to NSAIDs and physiotherapy. The age group and relief with conservative measures favours disc herniation over sinister causes like malignancy.

stem: Which of the following requires urgent ophthalmology referral?
explanation: CRVO is an ophthalmic emergency presenting with sudden painless visual loss and classic 'blood and thunder' fundus (flame haemorrhages in all quadrants, disc swelling, dilated tortuous veins). Urgent referral is required for assessment and treatment to prevent neovascular glaucoma.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents with SOB on exertion and peripheral oedema. No past or family history. ECG shows low voltage complexes. Echo reveals biventricular hypertrophy and dilated atria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The combination of low voltage on ECG with biventricular hypertrophy on echo is classic for cardiac amyloidosis ('voltage-mass mismatch'). In hypertensive heart disease, ECG would show LVH (high voltage). Amyloid infiltration causes thickening without electrical mass, hence low voltage despite structural hypertrophy.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with difficulty concentrating and speech difficulty. No recreational drug use or family history. Examination reveals 4cm splenomegaly. Labs: Albumin 32, Bilirubin 16, ALT 105. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. It presents in young patients with hepatic dysfunction (elevated ALT, low albumin) AND neuropsychiatric features (cognitive/speech difficulties). Splenomegaly indicates portal hypertension. Look for Kayser-Fleischer rings. Serum caeruloplasmin is low.

stem: A patient with SLE on prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine continues to have painful joints and pleuritic chest pain with no improvement. What is the most appropriate next management?
explanation: In SLE refractory to steroids and hydroxychloroquine, Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) is the preferred steroid-sparing agent, especially if there is renal involvement (lupus nephritis). MMF inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, reducing lymphocyte proliferation. It is superior to azathioprine for induction therapy in lupus nephritis.

stem: A 64-year-old lady with intractable vomiting is dehydrated. Labs: Na+ 131, K+ 3.3, Cl- 80, HCO3 high, Urea high, Creatinine normal. What is the appropriate fluid replacement?
explanation: This patient has hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis due to vomiting (loss of HCl from stomach). Features: low Cl-, high HCO3, low-normal Na+, low K+. Treatment is isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl) to replenish chloride, correct alkalosis and restore volume. Potassium supplementation should be added given K+ 3.3.

stem: What is the main cause of death in Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome?
explanation: VHL syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutation in the VHL tumour suppressor gene. Manifestations include clear cell RCC, cerebellar and retinal haemangioblastomas, phaeochromocytoma, and pancreatic cysts. RCC is the leading cause of death in VHL, occurring in up to 70% of patients.

stem: A 60-year-old retired shipyard worker presents with 3-month history of cough, haemoptysis and weight loss. Serum Na+ 130, K+ 3.5, normal creatinine and urea. CXR shows left hilar mass with lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is strongly associated with smoking. It classically causes central/hilar masses with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Hyponatraemia here is due to SIADH (paraneoplastic syndrome), which is most commonly associated with SCLC. Shipyard workers have asbestos exposure risk (mesothelioma) but the SIADH + central mass points to SCLC.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with pain in small joints, fingers turning blue on exposure to cold (Raynaud's), oral ulcers and facial rash. Which antibody is most likely to be present?
explanation: The clinical picture — small joint arthralgia, Raynaud's phenomenon, oral ulcers, and facial (malar) rash — is classic for SLE. ANA is the best screening test for SLE, present in >95% of cases. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are more specific. Anti-CCP = RA; U1-RNP = MCTD; Scl-70 = systemic sclerosis; Anti-Jo-1 = myositis.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with recurrent visible haematuria. He is otherwise well and all examinations are unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Classic presentation: young adult male with recurrent episodes of macroscopic haematuria, often concurrent with or shortly after an URTI ('synpharyngitic haematuria'). Anti-GBM causes rapidly progressive GN; membranous GN causes nephrotic syndrome; PSGN follows streptococcal infection by 2-3 weeks.

stem: A man with type 1 DM presents with gradually worsening vomiting episodes over 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Diabetic gastroparesis is a complication of longstanding diabetes (type 1 > type 2) caused by autonomic neuropathy affecting gastric motility. It presents with nausea, vomiting, bloating, early satiety, and postprandial fullness. Diagnosis is confirmed by gastric emptying scintigraphy. Treatment: metoclopramide, domperidone, erythromycin.

stem: After a road traffic accident with massive haemorrhage, which blood product must be administered before the patient's Rh status is known?
explanation: In massive haemorrhage when Rh status is unknown, O-negative red cells are given for RBCs. Cryoprecipitate and FFP do not contain red blood cells and therefore carry no Rh antigens — they can be given regardless of Rh status. Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII — crucial in massive haemorrhage coagulopathy.

stem: A 34-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis presents with worsening shortness of breath. PFTs show: reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, reduced KCO with normal TLCO. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bronchiolitis obliterans (BO) associated with RA shows: obstructive pattern (reduced FEV1/FVC), with reduced KCO (gas transfer coefficient) but NORMAL TLCO. This pattern of 'isolated KCO reduction' with obstruction is characteristic of BO/obliterative bronchiolitis. Emphysema would show reduced TLCO. Sarcoidosis is typically restrictive.

stem: A 21-year-old female with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) caused by Robertsonian translocation. Which investigation is most relevant to confirm this?
explanation: Robertsonian translocation is a chromosomal structural abnormality where two acrocentric chromosomes fuse. In Down syndrome caused by translocation (vs trisomy 21), standard karyotyping (46 chromosomes but with an extra chromosome 21 fused to another, e.g., chromosome 14) is the definitive investigation. This is also important for parental testing and recurrence risk assessment.

stem: A young rugby player collapses with a low heart rate during exercise. What is the most likely underlying reason?
explanation: HOCM is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Dynamic obstruction worsens with exercise (increased heart rate, decreased preload/afterload). Exertion causes decreased cardiac output, syncope, and potentially ventricular fibrillation. The low heart rate may represent a reflex bradycardia post-collapse. ECG typically shows LVH with repolarisation changes.

stem: A 30-year-old female presents with arthralgias, oral ulcers and genital ulcers. Which HLA type is most associated?
explanation: Behçet's disease classically presents with the triad of oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. It is strongly associated with HLA-B51. Other features include skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis), arthritis, and vascular/neurological involvement. More common in Middle Eastern and Asian populations.

stem: An 81-year-old man with memory problems, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence is diagnosed with Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH). Where does CSF absorption normally occur?
explanation: CSF is produced by the choroid plexus (lateral, third, and fourth ventricles). CSF absorption occurs at the arachnoid granulations (villi) in the superior sagittal sinus. In NPH, there is impaired CSF absorption leading to ventricular dilatation without raised ICP. Classic triad: 'Wet, Wacky, Wobbly' — urinary incontinence, dementia, gait ataxia.

stem: A patient has a prolonged QTc of 510ms. What is the underlying mechanism of this ECG change?
options: Delayed conduction to bundle of His
explanation: Prolonged QT interval results from abnormal cardiac repolarisation, most commonly due to dysfunction of potassium channels (IKr channels encoded by KCNH2/hERG gene). This delays repolarisation and extends the action potential duration. QTc >500ms carries significant risk of Torsades de Pointes. Causes: congenital (Romano-Ward, Jervell-Lange-Nielsen) or acquired (drugs, electrolyte abnormalities).

stem: A 19-year-old develops a rash after taking amoxicillin for an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Amoxicillin/ampicillin given to a patient with EBV (infectious mononucleosis) causes a widespread maculopapular rash in ~90% of cases. The URTI symptoms (sore throat, malaise, lymphadenopathy) with a young patient should raise suspicion of glandular fever before prescribing amoxicillin. This is not a true drug allergy — Monospot/Paul-Bunnell test and EBV serology should be checked.

stem: A patient has undergone total parathyroidectomy. Calcium is 1.97 mmol/L. What is the next step?
explanation: After total parathyroidectomy (e.g., for tertiary hyperparathyroidism in CKD), 'hungry bone syndrome' occurs — the bones rapidly uptake calcium causing severe hypocalcaemia. Ca2+ 1.97 is symptomatic/dangerous. IV calcium gluconate is required urgently. Oral calcium is insufficient for this acute drop. Hungry bone syndrome can last days to weeks requiring high-dose IV then oral calcium.

stem: A 52-year-old male with 2-week headaches, hypertension, bilateral renal cysts. Mother has hypertension. Labs show deranged creatinine. What is the most likely cause of the deranged renal function?
explanation: ADPKD (PKD1/PKD2 mutation) is the most common inherited kidney disease. Features: bilateral renal cysts, hypertension, haematuria, flank pain, and progressive CKD. Family history of hypertension/renal disease is common. Intracranial berry aneurysms occur in ~10%. The bilateral renal cysts causing mass effect and progressive replacement of renal parenchyma explain the deranged RFTs.

stem: A patient on Ramipril (ACEi) for 4 weeks has K+ 6.8, Creatinine 178. She has DM and CKD. What is the most likely mechanism of hyperkalaemia?
options: Decreased K+ secretion in collecting duct (reduced aldosterone effect)
explanation: ACEi reduces angiotensin II → reduces aldosterone → less Na+/K+ exchange in collecting duct → K+ retention (hyperkalaemia). In CKD + DM patients, this risk is higher due to baseline hyporeninism (Type 4 RTA). K+ 6.8 is dangerous — ECG monitoring and stopping/reducing ACEi with urgent management required.

stem: A female at 30 weeks gestation presents with jaundice and pruritus. ALT 105, Bilirubin >50. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: ICP (obstetric cholestasis) presents in the third trimester with pruritus (especially palms/soles, worse at night) and jaundice, with elevated bile acids and liver enzymes. Bilirubin >50 and ALT ~100 fit ICP. HELLP would show haemolysis + thrombocytopenia. AFLP presents with coagulopathy + hypoglycaemia. ICP carries risk of stillbirth — ursodeoxycholic acid is treatment.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Denosumab?
explanation: Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that inhibits RANK-L, preventing RANK-L from binding to its receptor RANK on osteoclast precursors. This reduces osteoclast differentiation, function, and survival, thereby decreasing bone resorption. Used in osteoporosis, bone metastases, and giant cell tumour of bone.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Rituximab?
explanation: Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody targeting CD20, a surface antigen expressed on B lymphocytes (pre-B to mature B cells, but not plasma cells). It causes B cell depletion via complement-dependent cytotoxicity, ADCC, and apoptosis. Used in: NHL, CLL, RA, ANCA vasculitis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, ITP.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Ciclosporin?
explanation: Ciclosporin inhibits calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation of NFAT (Nuclear Factor of Activated T cells). This blocks IL-2 transcription, inhibiting T cell activation and proliferation. Used in: transplant rejection, psoriasis, RA, nephrotic syndrome, IBD. Note: the answer stated 'Anti-IL2 monoclonal antibody' — this is incorrect terminology; Ciclosporin is a calcineurin inhibitor that suppresses IL-2 production.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Adalimumab?
explanation: Adalimumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha, neutralising its pro-inflammatory effects. Used in: RA, psoriatic arthritis, AS, Crohn's disease, UC, psoriasis, uveitis. Other anti-TNF agents: infliximab (chimeric), etanercept (fusion protein), certolizumab, golimumab.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Apomorphine?
explanation: Apomorphine is a potent non-selective dopamine receptor agonist (D1 and D2 receptors). It is used as a rescue therapy in Parkinson's disease for 'off' episodes when oral medications fail. Given subcutaneously. Side effects include nausea (pretreat with domperidone), postural hypotension, and neuropsychiatric effects.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of Raltegravir?
explanation: Raltegravir is an HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI). It blocks the integrase enzyme that catalyses the insertion of HIV DNA into the host cell genome. This prevents viral replication. Other INSTIs: elvitegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir. Used as part of combination antiretroviral therapy (cART).

stem: A 32-year-old male has a routine health check for employment. He has no complaints. Urinalysis shows RBC ++. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Asymptomatic microscopic haematuria (AMH) in a young adult without risk factors: first step is to repeat urine analysis (ideally x2-3 times) to confirm persistent haematuria before proceeding to further investigation. Transient haematuria can occur after exercise, UTI, or menstruation. If confirmed persistent, further investigation (urine cytology, USS, cystoscopy) is warranted.

stem: A 65-year-old female has slurred speech, is responsive only to painful stimuli. Serum glucose is 1.4 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: This is severe hypoglycaemia with altered consciousness — oral glucose is unsafe (aspiration risk), IM glucagon is slower. IV 50% dextrose (dextrose 50%) provides rapid correction of critically low blood glucose. Give 50ml IV bolus of 50% glucose. If IV access unavailable, IM glucagon 1mg is the alternative. After recovery, identify and treat the cause.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with redness and tenderness on both cheeks, forehead and chin with erythema, papules and pustules. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Rosacea presents with facial flushing, erythema, papules, pustules and telangiectasia, typically on the central face (cheeks, nose, forehead, chin). Unlike acne vulgaris, there are no comedones. Treatment: topical metronidazole or azelaic acid for mild-moderate disease; oral doxycycline for more severe cases. Triggers: alcohol, spicy food, sun, heat.

stem: A lady with melena is on warfarin therapy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Warfarin-induced major/life-threatening bleeding (melena with active haemorrhage) requires immediate reversal. FFP contains all clotting factors including II, VII, IX, X (vitamin K-dependent). For urgent reversal: IV Vitamin K 5-10mg + 4-factor PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate) is actually first-line in life-threatening bleeding; FFP is second-line. Warfarin should also be stopped.

stem: What is the most common cardiac abnormality in Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)?
explanation: The most common congenital heart defect in Down syndrome is AVSD (also called atrioventricular canal defect or endocardial cushion defect), accounting for ~40-45% of cardiac defects in trisomy 21. It involves defects in both atrial and ventricular septa plus abnormal AV valves. VSD is the most common CHD overall in the general population but AVSD is most common specifically in Down syndrome.

stem: A 57-year-old male smoker with 10 pints alcohol/week presents with recurrent vertigo, worse when rotating his head in bed. What is the treatment?
explanation: BPPV (Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo) is characterised by brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head movement (especially rolling in bed). Caused by otolith debris (canalith) in the semicircular canals. Diagnosed with Dix-Hallpike test (positive = nystagmus). Treatment: Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning) — highly effective (~80% cure rate). Semont maneuver is an alternative.

stem: What is the classic side effect of fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin)?
explanation: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are associated with tendinopathy and tendon rupture, most commonly the Achilles tendon. Risk is increased in patients >60 years, on corticosteroids, or with renal failure. Other side effects: QT prolongation, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, photosensitivity, and Clostridioides difficile infection.

stem: Which food cannot be taken with statins?
explanation: Grapefruit contains furanocoumarins that inhibit CYP3A4 in the gut wall. Statins metabolised by CYP3A4 (simvastatin, atorvastatin, lovastatin) have significantly increased plasma levels when taken with grapefruit, increasing the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are not affected (not CYP3A4 substrates).

stem: What is the treatment for restless leg syndrome (RLS)?
explanation: Restless Legs Syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease) is treated with dopamine agonists as first-line: Ropinirole or Pramipexole. If secondary to iron deficiency, iron supplementation is the primary treatment. Gabapentin/pregabalin is used for RLS with pain. Avoid dopamine agonists in patients with impulse control disorders. Augmentation (worsening with dopaminergic therapy) is a long-term concern.

stem: A 56-year-old patient presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice and new-onset diabetes. CT shows a double duct sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The double duct sign (simultaneous dilation of both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct) on imaging is classic for pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. The tumour obstructs both ducts. Clinical features: painless jaundice (Courvoisier's sign — palpable non-tender gallbladder), weight loss, new-onset DM, and abdominal pain. CA 19-9 is the tumour marker.

stem: A 45-year-old Afro-Caribbean patient presents with BP 145/90. What is the most appropriate antihypertensive?
explanation: NICE guidelines for hypertension: For patients <55 years who are NOT Black African/Caribbean: start with ACEi or ARB. For patients of Black African/Caribbean origin at any age, or patients >55 years: start with a CCB (e.g., Amlodipine). This is because ACE inhibitors are less effective in this population due to low-renin hypertension.

stem: What must be checked before starting Azathioprine?
explanation: TPMT is the enzyme that metabolises azathioprine (and other thiopurines like 6-mercaptopurine). Patients with low or absent TPMT activity cannot metabolise these drugs efficiently, leading to accumulation of toxic metabolites causing severe myelosuppression. TPMT genotyping or enzyme activity assay must be checked before starting azathioprine. Dose reduction is required in intermediate metabolisers.

stem: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops jaundice. Which investigation is most appropriate?
explanation: UC is associated with Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) — a chronic cholestatic liver disease with multifocal bile duct strictures. PSC presents with jaundice, pruritus, and cholestatic LFTs (raised ALP, GGT). MRCP is the non-invasive investigation of choice showing beaded appearance of bile ducts. ERCP is therapeutic (not first-line diagnostic due to complication risk). pANCA is often positive.

stem: A patient with polypharmacy recently started treatment for hepatitis. Which drug is most likely responsible for causing depression?
explanation: Interferon-alpha (used in hepatitis B and C treatment) has well-known neuropsychiatric side effects including depression, anxiety, irritability, cognitive impairment, and suicidal ideation. This is a major dose-limiting side effect. Patients should be screened for depression before starting and monitored throughout. Contraindicated in patients with severe psychiatric illness.

stem: An autosomal dominant condition shows younger age of onset in successive generations. What is the most likely explanation?
explanation: Anticipation refers to a genetic disorder presenting at an earlier age and/or with greater severity in successive generations. It is caused by expansion of unstable trinucleotide (triplet) repeats in the gene. Examples: Huntington's disease (CAG repeats), Myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeats), Fragile X (CGG repeats), Friedreich's ataxia. The repeat number expands during meiosis, especially in paternal transmission for HD.

stem: A patient has 6-7 bloody stools per day with extensive inflammation involving the rectum and gut. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Truelove & Witts criteria for severe UC: >6 bloody stools/day PLUS one of: pulse >90, temperature >37.8°C, Hb <10.5g/dL, ESR >30mm/hr. UC characteristically involves the rectum (always) and extends continuously proximally. Management of severe UC: IV hydrocortisone, IV fluids, nutritional support, consider ciclosporin/infliximab if not responding, surgical review.

stem: A patient with Myasthenia Gravis — which drug would worsen the condition?
explanation: Multiple drugs can worsen Myasthenia Gravis. Beta blockers impair neuromuscular transmission and can precipitate myasthenic crisis. Other drugs to avoid: aminoglycosides (gentamicin), fluoroquinolones, magnesium, chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, D-penicillamine, statins (rarely), and neuromuscular blocking agents. Digoxin and aspirin are generally safe in MG.

stem: An immunocompetent person is diagnosed with toxoplasmosis. How would you treat?
explanation: In immunocompetent adults, primary toxoplasmosis is usually self-limiting and does not require treatment. However, if symptomatic or severe, sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine (+ folinic acid) is the treatment of choice. In immunocompromised patients (HIV with CD4 <200), treatment is mandatory. Co-trimoxazole is used for prophylaxis in HIV. In pregnancy, spiramycin reduces vertical transmission.

stem: What is the most common bias in meta-analysis?
explanation: Publication bias is the most significant bias in meta-analysis — studies with positive/significant results are more likely to be published than those with null or negative results. This leads to overestimation of treatment effects in meta-analyses. Detected by: funnel plot asymmetry, Egger's test, Begg's test. Other biases in systematic reviews: language bias, citation bias, multiple publication bias.

stem: A young male presents with oedema, hypoalbuminaemia, and urine protein +++. He develops DVT. What is the most likely cause of the thrombosis?
explanation: Nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema) causes urinary loss of many proteins including antithrombin III (ATIII — a natural anticoagulant). Loss of ATIII leads to a hypercoagulable state with risk of arterial and venous thrombosis (DVT, PE, renal vein thrombosis). Protein C and S are also lost but ATIII loss is the predominant mechanism for thrombosis in nephrotic syndrome.

stem: An elderly male has a right-sided pleural effusion with pleural fluid protein 4.8 g/dL. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Pleural fluid protein 4.8 g/dL = exudate (Light's criteria: protein >3.0 g/dL or pleural:serum protein ratio >0.5). Constrictive pericarditis causes elevated systemic venous pressure and impaired lymphatic drainage → exudative right-sided or bilateral effusion. Right-sided effusion is more common in constrictive pericarditis. Kussmaul's sign, pericardial knock, and diastolic equalisation on echo are other features.

stem: What is the tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)?
explanation: AFP is the primary tumour marker for HCC. It is elevated in ~70% of HCC cases. Levels >400 ng/mL are diagnostic of HCC in the appropriate clinical context (cirrhosis + hepatic mass). AFP is also elevated in: germ cell tumours (non-seminomatous), hepatoblastoma, and benign conditions (hepatitis, cirrhosis). Surveillance: 6-monthly USS ± AFP in cirrhotic patients.

stem: An elderly patient presents with facial flushing, diarrhoea, weight loss and palpitations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Carcinoid syndrome occurs when serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumours (usually midgut) metastasise to the liver, bypassing first-pass metabolism. Classic triad: episodic flushing, secretory diarrhoea, and bronchospasm. Right-sided valvular heart disease (carcinoid heart disease) is a serious complication. Investigation: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA, serum chromogranin A. Treatment: Octreotide/Lanreotide.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with backache and stiffness with some improvement with painkillers and exercise. Examination shows reduced forward flexion and lateral flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: AS (axial spondyloarthropathy) typically affects young males <40 years with inflammatory back pain: insidious onset, morning stiffness >1 hour, improves with exercise (not rest), worse at night. Reduced spinal mobility (Schober's test), bamboo spine on X-ray (late). Associated with HLA-B27 (~90%). Complications: uveitis, aortic regurgitation, restrictive lung disease, IgA nephropathy.

stem: An elderly male presents with recurrent painless haematuria. Examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Painless haematuria in an elderly patient is bladder cancer until proven otherwise. TCC (urothelial carcinoma) is the most common bladder cancer (~90%). Risk factors: smoking (most important), aniline dyes, cyclophosphamide, chronic UTI (→ squamous cell carcinoma). Investigation: urine cytology, cystoscopy (gold standard). SCC is associated with schistosomiasis and chronic irritation.

stem: A female with ANA positive and decreased C3 and C4 complement levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: SLE classically causes complement consumption (low C3 and C4) due to immune complex deposition and complement activation. ANA is positive in >95% of SLE. Low C3/C4 with ANA positivity is the characteristic pattern. In lupus flares, complement levels fall further. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are more specific. C4 is specifically low in early complement pathway defects associated with SLE.
